newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK-listed China firms untouched by Deng death.
newsitem.headline: HK-listed China firms untouched by Deng death.

text.p: Hong Kong-listed Chinese firms should benefit from China's positive economic outlook, which should remain unchanged following the death of patriarch Deng Xiaoping, analysts said on Monday.
"We look at the companies' earnings and growth, and Deng's death will not change our evaluation of these companies," said H-share analyst Andrew Kuet at Morgan Grenfell Asia Securities.
H-shares are stocks of mainland Chinese companies listed in Hong Kong.

On Monday, the H-share index outperformed the Hang Seng Index with a jump of 25.74 points or 2.71 percent to close at 973.91. The blue-chip index was off 69.16 points or 0.51 percent to close at 13,375.69.
But analysts said investors would remain wary of Chinese stocks that did well based on their political connections and would focus on corporate earnings.
The key to H-share vitality lay in reforming China's ailing state-run sector, China watchers agreed.
"If political uncertainty (after Deng's death) somehow affects the state sector reforms, then H-shares could be hit hard," one analyst said.

But overall, the economic outlook remained positive, observers said. By the time the paramount leader died, China had attained strong economic growth and curbed inflation while the currency had stabilised and foreign exchange reserves were growing, they said.
On Friday, China announced its economy would remain stable after Deng's death, growing by at least eight percent in 1997.
There would be no major adverse impacts on the economy because of Deng's passing, said Qiu Xiaohua, chief economist at the State Statistical Bureau.
Analysts often use China's gross domestic product target growth as a base to assess the development of various Chinese companies listed in Hong Kong, Kuet said.

Although the state sector companies -- and thereby H-shares -- have suffered under China's three-year austerity plan, most observers agree that the belt-tightening came to a gradual end by the last quarter of 1996.

"We are looking for a rebound in corporate earnings in the second half of 1997 and we are recommending our clients accumulate H-shares and B-shares (Chinese shares available to foreign investors)," another analyst said.
Hong Kong analysts saw the positive economic outlook leading to more H-share listings.
"H-share listings are approved according to a (Securities Commission of the State Council) programme, which will certainly continue," one said.
Consulting firm Arthur Andersen estimated last month that about 40 Chinese enterprises were lining up to launch initial public offerings in Hong Kong.
But other analysts noted that political decisions relating to investment in specific sectors may plague H-share companies, such as those in the power equipment business.
"For example, how many power projects are being reviewed (by the Chinese government) and how many will be approved? That would affect the industry," said one economist.
